wine.name: Blandy's 10 Year Old Malmsey
wine.grapes: Malvasia alone, the grape sold in English as Malmsey.
wine.sites: Malvasia bought from growers on the island's terraced vineyards, then aged in Blandy's Wine Lodge in the centre of Funchal, the São Francisco lodge, named for the Franciscan convent on whose site it stands.
wine.making: The Malvasia is fermented with its own yeasts and fortified with grape spirit early, which keeps much of its sugar. Canteiro ageing follows, in seasoned oak casks under the warm roof of the lodge, and the wines blended for bottling average ten years of age, by the house's account.
wine.glass: Deep amber; honey, caramel, sweet confectionery and tea leaf over walnut and a breath of smoked wood. Sweet, soft and full, kept fresh by the high acidity of Madeira, with a long finish that recalls old brandy.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink when it is bottled, and it holds for years in bottle; once opened it keeps for months, which suits a bottle poured by the glass.
wine.serve: About 16 degrees Celsius, slightly cool, as the house advises; no need to decant; a small white wine glass, after dinner or with dessert.

label.means: The English name for Malvasia, the sweetest of the four noble grapes of Madeira.
An age statement for a blend of wines of several ages, averaging about ten years, as the house describes it.
The protected name of the island's fortified wine; its unfortified wines carry another, Madeirense.

records.table: Blandy's 10 Year Old Malmsey is the sweet Malvasia of the family house founded in Funchal in 1811, aged for years in oak casks under the warm roof of its lodge. Honey, caramel and walnut are kept fresh by acidity; pour it slightly cool after dinner.
records.story: John Blandy (1783 to 1855) came to Madeira from England in 1808 with a letter of introduction to the island's wine merchants, and in 1811 he set up on his own, with two of his brothers, as a wine shipper and general trader. The house tells of a trade that reached Russia, northern Europe, the West Indies and North America. On his death in 1855 his son took charge. In the nineteenth century the family gathered buildings on the site of the Franciscan convent of São Francisco into the lodge where its fine wines age. In 1913 a group of shippers formed the Madeira Wine Association to pool their resources; Blandy's joined in 1925, and in 1981 the association took the name Madeira Wine Company. In 1989 the family took the Symington family, Port shippers of Oporto, into partnership, and in 2011, its bicentenary year, an agreement gave the Blandys control of the company once more. The 10 Year Old Malmsey stands at the sweet end of the house's age ladder and is a ready way to show a guest what canteiro does: years of gentle warmth under a lodge roof, rather than months in a heated tank.

traps: Malmsey and Malvasia are one grape and one style: Malmsey is the English name the label prints, and it is the sweetest of the four noble grapes.
Canteiro is years of natural warmth in cask under the lodge roof; estufagem is at least three months in a tank heated to between 45 and 50 degrees Celsius. The 10 Year Old is canteiro.

report: Every fact rests on the house's own pages and the Madeira Wine Company's, read through search summaries; the regional government's culture page gives the convent and its suppression in 1835, and Visit Madeira and the British Historical Society of Portugal were read beside them.
John Blandy's dates and his son's succession in 1855 rest on the Blandy group's own timeline, with the British Historical Society of Portugal's account agreeing.

The story of John Blandy arriving as a quartermaster with Beresford's garrison of 1807, and the Napoleon cask of 1815, were met in one account each and are left out; the house's own page has him arrive in 1808 with a letter of introduction.
The dates of the family's purchases at São Francisco differ across pages (1824, 1838 and 1840), so the story says only the nineteenth century.
The 10 Year Old sheet names no vineyards; a house sheet for a single harvest Malmsey of 1996 names São Jorge on the north coast, which is left out as it may not hold for the blend.
The house's sheet advises 16 degrees Celsius; the regional government's guidance gives 13 to 14 for younger Madeira and 15 to 16 for older, so the record keeps the house's figure.
The casks are seasoned oak on the 10 Year Old sheet; the lodge's casks are mostly American oak by other pages, which the record does not claim for this wine.
Searches for this record: 8 of the group's 32, with 2 more shared by the group on the island's rules and its guidance on service; one fetch of the Madeira Wine Company's site was refused.

changed: wine.sites: the lodge was named for the Franciscan convent that once stood beside it; now for the convent on whose site it stands, since the regional government's culture page has the lodge's buildings as largely all that remains of the convent, and a travel guide puts the lodge on the convent's grounds.

wine.making: moving down to cooler floors with time is cut; the house's 10 Year Old sheets give natural yeasts, early fortification, canteiro in seasoned oak and the average age of ten years, and the wine institute puts canteiro casks in the warm upper floors, but no source read gave the move downward.
story: the convent's suppression in 1835 is cut and the lodge now stands on the convent's site rather than beside it; no source read gave 1835.

story: the Association of 1913 was formed with exports in a slump to widen the shippers' reach abroad; now to pool their resources, as the company histories read give it (FundingUniverse, Encyclopedia.com), and the slump was in none of them.

story: by the late 1970s the Blandy family held the controlling share is cut; the accounts read give control after 1974 to the Blandy and Leacock families together, and one has the Blandys at just over 40 per cent; the story now gives the name Madeira Wine Company of 1981, in three company histories.
cards[1].back: the association later grew into the Madeira Wine Company; now took that name in 1981.
traps[1]: estufagem was heated to no more than 50 degrees; now between 45 and 50 degrees Celsius for at least three months, the wine institute's own figures.
questions[0].exp: the younger, simpler blends; now the younger blends, since simpler is a judgement no source gives.
open: The house's 10 Year Old sheets differ on the moment of fortification (about 48 hours into fermentation on one, after two to four days on another); the record says early and gives no figure.
The house's newer 10 Year Old sheet advises 16 degrees Celsius while its general Malmsey page says no higher than 15; the record keeps about 16, the sheet's figure.

wine.name: Henriques & Henriques 15 Year Old Verdelho
wine.grapes: Verdelho alone, the medium dry step of the four noble grapes.
wine.sites: Verdelho partly from the house's own vineyard at Quinta Grande above Câmara de Lobos, terraced between 350 and 700 metres and planted mostly with Verdelho, as the house and its importer tell it.
wine.making: The Verdelho is fermented and then fortified with neutral grape spirit while some sugar remains, which leaves it medium dry. It ages by canteiro, in oak casks warmed only by the climate in the house's lodges at Câmara de Lobos, and is bottled as a blend of wines of several ages carrying the 15 Years Old statement.
wine.glass: Dark gold with amber glints; raisin, honey, Seville orange and dried apricot over nuts and old wood. Medium dry, with caramel and nut on the palate and a keen acidity that lingers.
wine.ageing: Drinkable as soon as it is bottled and long lived after; an opened bottle keeps its character for months, so one bottle can serve many evenings.
wine.serve: 13 to 16 degrees Celsius, the island's guidance for Madeira, the older the wine the warmer; decanting is unnecessary; a small white wine glass, as an aperitif.

label.means: The noble grape of the medium dry style, between Sercial and Boal on the ladder.
The wine's age statement: it names a blend of several ages, never a single harvest.
The house name, from two sons of the founder who joined in partnership after his death in 1912.

records.table: A Câmara de Lobos house of 1850 that grows Verdelho on its own terraces, Henriques & Henriques ages its 15 Year Old Verdelho slowly in cask. A little cool and medium dry, it makes an aperitif, with orange peel, raisin and nuts cut by sharp acidity.
records.story: A man of an old landowning family of Câmara de Lobos, settled on the south coast west of Funchal for generations, set up the firm in 1850, the year the house gives for its founding. It was a hard time to begin: oidium struck the island's vines in the early 1850s and phylloxera in 1872. When the founder died in 1912 two of his sons joined in partnership, and the firm took the name it carries, Henriques & Henriques; in 1913 the family's holdings were gathered into one company, and from 1925, the house says, it shipped its own wines abroad. Unlike most Madeira shippers, which buy their grapes from the island's many smallholders, the house has long farmed substantial vineyards of its own around Câmara de Lobos. In 1992 it began a programme of growth, building a new ageing cellar at Câmara de Lobos and a winemaking centre on its land at Quinta Grande, where its largest vineyard is planted mostly with Verdelho. Its 15 Year Old range, one bottling for each noble grape, lets a student taste the ladder side by side, and the Verdelho is the middle step: drier than Boal, softer than Sercial, a medium dry Madeira that shows how much acidity the island's wines keep after years in cask.

The founder and his two sons are described, not named: the house's pages give his death in 1912 but no birth year for him, and no dates for the sons.
Canteiro ageing and neutral grape spirit rest on the importer's page; Hedonism's page agrees on fifteen years of canteiro, and the house's own sheet gives the tasting note but not the method.
The fruit from Quinta Grande rests on the importer's page; the house's own page says the vineyard is planted mostly with Verdelho, so the sites line is hedged.

The library's trap that Madeira age statements are minimums for the blend sits uneasily with Blandy's sheet (an average age of ten years) and the regional government's page (a blend of wines of several ages); this record says only a blend of several ages.
A sale of the house to a French spirits group was not searched and is left out of the story.
Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 32.

changed: story: oidium struck the island's vines in 1852; now in the early 1850s, since outside histories (GuildSomm, the Madeira Wine Guide, CellarTracker's region article) give 1851 for its arrival and the regional government the middle of the century, while only the house's page gives 1852. Phylloxera in 1872 stands in most accounts.
open: The founder's full name differs (João Gonçalves Henriques in most accounts, João Joaquim Gonçalves Henriques in one); he stays described, not named, as the author chose.

wine.name: Barbeito Malvasia 20 Years Old
wine.grapes: Malvasia alone, the sweetest of the four noble grapes.
wine.sites: Malvasia from the north coast at São Jorge and Arco de São Jorge, with fruit from Fajã dos Padres on the south coast in some lots, by the house's lot sheets.
wine.making: Fermentation is stopped with grape spirit at 96 per cent, which leaves the wine sweet. Years by canteiro follow in oak casks, French oak in the lots the house details, under the warmth of the lodge, before it is bottled in numbered lots without caramel for colour.
wine.glass: Amber; toffee, nuts, smoke and a resinous hint of pine, with lime peel at the edge. Sweet but never heavy: a high, cutting acidity carries it long and leaves it fresh.
wine.ageing: Sound in bottle for many years, though ready on release; an opened bottle holds up for months. Lots differ a little, so the lot number tells one bottling from the next.
wine.serve: 15 to 16 degrees Celsius, the island's guidance for older Madeira; a blend needs no decanting; a small white wine glass and a small measure.

label.means: The sweetest noble grape, Malmsey in English; Barbeito prints the Portuguese name.
One age statement over a blend of many harvests, not the wine of a single year.
The number of the bottling: the 20 Years Old is released in separate lots that differ a little.

records.table: No caramel goes into Barbeito Malvasia 20 Years Old: the Câmara de Lobos firm founded in 1946 ages it many years in cask and bottles it in numbered lots. Toffee and smoke meet lime peel and a cutting acidity in a sweet wine; pour a small measure.
records.story: A collector of books on the island's history and on Columbus, as the house recalls him, Mário Barbeito de Vasconcelos (1905 to 1985), born in Funchal, founded Vinhos Barbeito in 1946. Its importer describes those years as a difficult moment for a new Madeira house. After his death in 1985 his daughter, who had worked in the firm since 1976, ran the house, and her son joined her in 1989. In 1991 the Kinoshita family, who had sold Barbeito's wines in Japan since 1967, joined the house in a joint venture, and in the early 1990s the founder's grandson took charge of the house and its winemaking. He stopped colouring the wines with caramel, began in 1995 to age Tinta Negra by canteiro, and, on the house's own word, was the first to name that red grape on a Madeira label. Barbeito became known for wines bottled as the casks made them, for single casks and for numbered lots. Its Malvasia 20 Years Old, released lot by lot from north coast fruit, shows that clarity in a sweet wine: rich, yet sharp enough to end cleanly, proof that a sweet Madeira need not be heavy.

Bottled without caramel, a Barbeito can look paler than another house's Madeira of the same age; the colour is no sign of youth.

The daughter and the grandson are living or may be, so neither is named; the Japanese partner is named only as a family, and the wine O Japonês carries no personal name.
By the Rare Wine Co's account the founder had kept the books for another Madeira house before 1946 and bought old stocks from island families; one source only, so left out.

The sites and the making follow the house's sheets for lots 6072, 7199, 12089, 14050 and 18143, which differ: the record names the places they share and gives French oak only for the lots the house details.
The pick is sound: the 20 Years Old Malvasia is a standing bottling released lot by lot, reviewed under several lot numbers.

wine.name: D'Oliveira Frasqueira Boal
wine.classification: Frasqueira: one harvest of one noble grape, at least twenty years in wood
wine.grapes: Boal alone, the noble grape of the medium sweet style, spelt Bual in English.
wine.sites: Each bottling is one year's Boal; many of the family's old wines came from its own vineyards in São Martinho, a parish of Funchal, and they age in cask in its lodge in the Rua dos Ferreiros.
wine.making: Boal is fortified with grape spirit partway through fermentation, which leaves it medium sweet. The wine of one harvest then ages for at least twenty years in old oak casks in the lodge, often far longer, and the family bottles only what its orders need, printing the bottling year on the back label.
wine.glass: Dark amber; butter caramel, honey and fig with blood orange and clementine peel. Rich and medium sweet, with the weight of Boal, cut by a high acidity, and clean as it fades slowly.
wine.ageing: Ready when it leaves the cask after its decades in wood; a sound bottle lasts for decades more, and an opened one lives on for months.
wine.serve: 15 to 16 degrees Celsius, as the island advises for older Madeira; decant it, and draw an old cork with care, since it can crumble; a small white wine glass.

label.means: The Portuguese spelling of Bual, the noble grape of the medium sweet style.
One harvest of one noble grape, at least twenty years in wood; not every label prints the word.
Medium sweet: the sweetness the rules tie to Boal, in Portuguese and often in English beside it.

records.table: One harvest of Boal, kept in cask by a Funchal family that bottles its old vintages only to order: that is D'Oliveira Frasqueira Boal. Medium sweet, with caramel, fig and orange peel and a high acidity, it is decanted and poured cellar cool.
records.story: Pereira d'Oliveira is a family house of Funchal whose beginnings are told in more than one way. Most accounts date it to 1850, while its American importer traces the company's origin to the 1880s and to a landowner and grower of São Martinho, a parish on the city's western side, where the family's vineyards gave many of its old wines. The family kept its single harvests apart in cask, holding that Madeira ages better in wood than in glass, and bottled only what its orders needed. So its lodge in the Rua dos Ferreiros of old Funchal came to hold wines reaching far back: Verdelho of 1850, which its importer traces to the São Martinho vineyards, Boal from the first years of the twentieth century, each sold as a Frasqueira with its bottling year printed on the back label. Under the island's rules a Frasqueira is one harvest of one noble grape aged at least twenty years in wood, and the house's often wait far longer. Its Boal of 1908 has been bottled a century and more after its harvest. Taste one to learn what time in cask does to Madeira: rich, yet fresh after a hundred years.

others.name: D'Oliveira Frasqueira Verdelho

The year on the front of a Frasqueira is the harvest, not the bottling: a Boal of 1908 may have been bottled a century later.
A Frasqueira needs at least twenty years in wood; a Colheita, also from one harvest, needs only five.

report: The house's own site was not found by search, so every fact rests on two secondary sources or on the library's rule for Frasqueira and Colheita (twenty years and five, from the region record).

Founded is left empty: 1850 in most accounts (the Madeira Wine Guide, the Big Fortified Tasting), 1820 in one, and the 1880s in the Rare Wine Co's profile; the story says the beginnings are told two ways, and the founder is not named for want of dates.

The bottling year on the back label rests on the Madeira Wine Guide and a Portuguese merchant's listing of the 1850 Verdelho, bottled in 2015; its exact wording is not put on the label list, and Meio Doce rests on listings of the 1908 and 1980 Boals.

Old wines kept in old oak and bottled only to order rest on the Big Fortified Tasting's directory and the Madeira Wine Guide; the house's acquisitions of other firms (one list, with Barros e Sousa in 2013) and the date of 1619 for the lodge building rest on one source each and are left out.
The glass draws on notes of the 1958 Boal and other D'Oliveiras Boals; the Frasqueiras run across many vintages and no single one is described.
The plan names the wine D'Oliveira Frasqueira Boal; labels print D'Oliveiras and the grape with its harvest year.
Searches for this record: 8 of the group's 32, two of them returning nothing of use.

story: a Boal of 1908 may leave the cask a century after its harvest; now its Boal of 1908 has been bottled a century and more after, since bottlings of that wine are recorded in 2008, 2015 and 2023 (CellarTracker, a merchant, a tasting forum).

open: Founded stays empty: 1850 (Benchmark Wine, Winebid, the Madeira Wine Guide), 1820 (Berry Bros and Rudd) and the 1880s (the Rare Wine Co) all stand in print.

wine.grapes: Malvasia only, bought from the island's growers.
wine.sites: Growers across the island sell the house its Malvasia, since it farms no vineyards of its own; the wine ages in its lodge in the Rua 31 de Janeiro in Funchal, once a cereal mill.
wine.making: Fermentation at a controlled temperature gives way to fortification with grape spirit, which keeps its sweetness. The wine then rests by canteiro in French and American oak casks under the lodge roof; the blend bottled under the 15 Years Old statement draws on wines of several ages.
wine.glass: Amber in colour; vanilla, caramel and nuts on the nose, then dried fig, raisin and chocolate. Sweet and full, with molasses on the finish and Madeira's acidity to lift it.
wine.ageing: It can be drunk from release or kept for years in bottle; once opened it lasts for months.
wine.serve: 13 to 14 degrees Celsius, as the house advises for its sweet Malvasia; there is nothing to decant; a small white wine glass, with dark chocolate or petits fours, as the house suggests.

label.means: The Portuguese name of Malmsey, the sweetest noble grape; some export labels print the English one.
The age the blend declares, drawn from wines of several ages rather than one harvest.
The founder's initials and surname; his family has run the house since 1877.

records.table: Since 1924 H.M. Borges, a Funchal family house of 1877 that buys its grapes, has aged its wines slowly in a former cereal mill, its 15 Year Old Malvasia among them. Sweet, with caramel, fig and chocolate held up by acidity, it belongs beside dessert or dark chocolate.
records.story: Initials and a surname make the house's name, those of a Funchal merchant who in 1877 set out, in the house's version, to seek wines from across the island and age them. Its first premises, nearer the centre of the city, lacked what shipping abroad required, and in 1924 it moved into a building that had been a mill for grinding cereal, fitting it out as a lodge while keeping its old walls; from there it became a producer and exporter in its own right. The house has stayed in the founder's family ever since. Like most Madeira shippers it owns no vineyards and buys from growers across the island, choosing by grape: Sercial, Verdelho, Boal, Malvasia and the red Tinta Negra. Its fine wines age by canteiro, the name taken from the wooden beams, canteiros, on which the casks rest, in French and American oak under the roof of the old mill. The house takes each of the four noble grapes to fifteen years, and the Malvasia is the one for dessert. It stands for the small family house outside the large companies that ages the island's sweet wine the slow way, and it gives a guest a sweet Madeira with acidity enough to leave the palate fresh.

traps: Sweet Madeira is served a little cool, not cold like Fino: the house advises 13 to 14 degrees Celsius for its Malvasia.
H.M. Borges of Funchal is a different house from Henriques & Henriques of Câmara de Lobos, though both are old family firms.

cards.front: H.M. Borges: how do its fine wines age, and in what wood?
cards.back: By canteiro, on wooden beams under the lodge roof, in French and American oak casks.

cards.back: From growers across the island: the house farms no vineyards of its own.

questions.q: The Funchal lodge that H.M. Borges moved into in 1924, becoming an exporter in its own right, had once served another purpose. What was it?
opts: A mill for grinding cereal
A Franciscan convent
A sugar cane mill
A Jesuit college
questions.exp: By the house's account the building was a cereal mill; the Franciscan convent of São Francisco gave its name to the Blandy lodge nearby.

report: The founding of 1877, the move of 1924, the cereal mill, the family's four generations and the grapes bought from growers rest on the house's own pages, with Visit Madeira and the Madeira Wine Guide agreeing on 1877, 1924 and the family; the mill rests on the house and its own company profile only.
The founder is described, not named: no dates for him were found in two sources.
The making (off the skins, temperature controlled, canteiro in oak) rests on the house's page and a merchant's sheet; French and American oak is the house's word alone.
The glass joins the house's note (vanilla, nuts, chocolate) and Decanter's (caramel, dried fig, raisin, molasses); some export bottlings print Malmsey rather than Malvasia.

The house's site styles the 15 Years Old Malvasia Reserve on one page and Special Reserve on others, while the regulations call a fifteen year wine Reserva Extra; no reserve term is put on the label list.

A possible swap for the checker: Cossart Gordon, by the Madeira Wine Company's own page the oldest Madeira house (1745), is a name a guest is likelier to know, but it shares the Madeira Wine Company with Blandy's; Justino's is the other candidate. The author keeps H.M. Borges, an independent family house with a full canteiro range.
Searches for this record: 4 of the group's 32.

changed: story: the founder's family had run the house through four generations; now the house has stayed in the founder's family ever since, since a count of generations moves with time.

wine.serve and table: blue cheese is gone; the house's page for the 15 Years Old Malvasia pairs it with dark or milk chocolate, pralinés and petits fours, and no source read paired it with blue cheese.
wine.glass: dark chocolate is now chocolate, the house's own note (chocolate and nuts on the palate).
wine.making: fermented off its skins is cut; a merchant's sheet gives fermentation under temperature control, but no source read gave the skins.

sources: Visit Madeira gives way to the house's FAQ, which gives 13 to 14 degrees Celsius for Boal and Malvasia, the figure the serve, the trap and the wine question rest on; the Madeira Wine Guide and an importer keep 1877 and 1924 in two outside sources.
open: The cereal mill rests on the house's pages and its own company profile only; it stays told as the house tells it.
One tourism listing gives the house a second address in Funchal; the Madeira Wine Guide and the house's profile give Rua 31 de Janeiro, which the record keeps.
